narrative: Star Vetter automatically identifies candidate eclipsing binary stars in data from NASA's TESS satellite. An eclipsing binary is a pair of stars orbiting each other in a way that causes periodic dips in brightness as one star passes in front of the other. The project begins with light curves - brightness measurements over time - from roughly 14,000 TESS targets. Each candidate undergoes statistical vetting to rule out noise and instrumental artifacts, then is cross-checked against six established catalogs of known variable stars to identify novel systems. Candidates that survive this automated filtering undergo a pixel-level check - an automated examination of the imaging data to confirm the signal originates from the target star itself and not nearby sources. Those that pass become confirmed candidates on this site. The project currently lists 205 confirmed candidates. All results come with open documentation of the vetting process so you can see exactly what was checked and understand the limitations of any individual candidate.

faqs.question: What is an eclipsing binary star?
faqs.answer: An eclipsing binary is a system of two stars orbiting each other. When their orbital plane is aligned with our view from Earth, one star periodically passes in front of the other, causing a small but measurable dip in the total brightness we receive. By studying the pattern, depth, and timing of these brightness dips, astronomers can learn about the stars' sizes, masses, and orbits.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a 'candidate' and a 'confirmed' result on this site?
faqs.answer: A candidate is a star whose light curve shows a pattern consistent with an eclipsing binary according to statistical tests. A confirmed result is a candidate that has passed Star Vetter's automated pixel-level check, which verifies that the brightness variations actually originate from the target star itself and are not caused by nearby stars or instrumental effects. 'Confirmed' here means it passed this project's pipeline - it does not imply that the result has been independently verified by other researchers or accepted into a scientific catalog.

faqs.question: What is the machine learning score I see on some candidates?
faqs.answer: Star Vetter includes a machine learning model trained on over 2,000 labeled examples to provide a second opinion on which candidates are most likely to be real eclipsing binaries. This score outperforms the rule-based baseline used in the main vetting pipeline. However, the ML score is provided for reference only; it does not currently gate which candidates get checked or determine which results appear on the site. All candidates that pass the statistical and novelty checks undergo the same pixel-level examination.

faqs.question: How does a candidate get checked for false alarms?
faqs.answer: Every candidate that passes statistical vetting and novelty cross-checking undergoes an automated pixel-level check. This process examines the imaging data to verify that the brightness dips come from the target star itself, not from a nearby star bleeding light into the photometry or other contamination. This is a fully automated examination, not a manual visual review. Candidates that pass this check are listed as confirmed on the site.

faqs.question: What if the eclipse period looks like it could be an alias?
faqs.answer: Star Vetter tests each candidate for period aliasing - the risk that the observed eclipse pattern actually represents half (or another fraction) of the true orbital period. The check compares the depth of odd-numbered eclipses against even-numbered eclipses; if these depths differ significantly, it suggests the candidate may be experiencing period confusion. When this test raises a concern, that caveat is noted on the candidate's page so you can see the open question alongside the data.

faqs.question: Can I verify a result myself?
faqs.answer: Yes. Each confirmed candidate is linked to its light curve data from TESS, which is publicly available. You can download the data and examine the brightness pattern yourself. Individual candidate pages include orbital period and eclipse depths measured from the light curve, along with all vetting details, so you have the information needed to form your own assessment.

faqs.question: What happens to a candidate after it appears on this site?
faqs.answer: Star Vetter's pipeline ends at the pixel-level check. Candidates listed here have not undergone follow-up spectroscopy, radial-velocity measurements, or other observations by professional astronomers. They have not been added to official catalogs or published in peer-reviewed journals through this project. The site serves as a resource for the community; what happens next - whether a candidate receives further study - depends on the interests and efforts of other researchers.
